publications.title: CP26/38: Financial Crime Guide updates
publications.text:
CP26/38: Financial Crime Guide updates
Consultation opens 23/10/2026. Consultation closes 24/12/2026.
We're consulting on changes to our Financial Crime Guide to help firms strengthen their systems and controls.
Why we're consulting
Firms are essential partners in tackling financial crime.
We want firms to keep detecting, preventing and disrupting financial crime, so we can protect consumers and maintain trust in the financial system.
We want our Financial Crime Guide to keep pace with emerging risks, such as those linked to AI, cryptoassets and evolving sanctions regimes.
We’re proposing changes to the following areas:
fraud
cryptoassets – to reflect new regime from October 2027
financial and trade sanctions
proliferation financing
data security
financial crime systems and controls
money laundering and terrorist financing
Who this is for
This consultation is relevant to all firms we supervise for financial crime, including under the Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and Transfer of Funds (Information on the Payer) Regulations 2017 (MLRs), such as:
Annex 1 financial institutions
cryptoasset businesses
It may also interest:
organisations working with these firms
financial services trade bodies
professional bodies
other parties interested in financial crime prevention, including non-governmental organisations and academics
Next steps
Please send us your feedback by 24 December 2026.
We'll consider all responses and publish feedback, along with the final Financial Crime Guide text, in a Policy Statement.
Future plans for the Financial Crime Guide
We are exploring ways to provide financial crime guidance that:
meets the needs of our wide-ranging and varied population
is focused on emerging risks and priority areas
allows for a range of feedback opportunities
This could include:
holding a series of question-and-answer sessions, either in person or online
publishing timely standalone guidance without prior consultation, where it is not required
This guidance would then be consolidated within the Financial Crime Guide at a future date.
Background
We last updated the Financial Crime Guide to reflect supervisory findings and changing risks.
Since then, the UK's sanctions regime has evolved, cryptoasset regulation has developed, and firms have increasingly adopted AI and third-party tools for financial crime controls.
These proposals support our objective of making sure markets function well, by reducing and preventing financial crime.
They're also relevant to our consumer protection and integrity objectives and compatible with our secondary objective on international competitiveness and growth.

publications.title: FCA restricts 6 firms following concerns over anti-money laundering controls
publications.text:
FCA restricts 6 firms following concerns over anti-money laundering controls
Restrictions have been placed on 6 unregulated lenders, known as Annex 1 firms, after the FCA raised concerns about their anti-money laundering policies, controls and procedures while assessing their applications.
The restrictions were imposed by the FCA on each firm’s request and limit their ability to take on new customers or do new business with existing customers, including extending existing credit.
This action forms part of the FCA’s enhanced oversight of Annex 1 firms. These firms operate in sectors that can present a heightened risk of money laundering and other financial crime and are required to register with the FCA for supervision under the Money Laundering Regulations. They are not authorised or subject to wider FCA regulation.
The FCA has previously warned Annex 1 firms that they will be subject to increased scrutiny. They must be able to demonstrate they understand the financial crime risks they face and have effective systems and controls in place to manage those risks, or face action.
More widely, the FCA is assessing responses to an information request sent to around 900 registered Annex 1 firms to identify and disrupt financial crime risks and determine where further action is needed.
The FCA has also reminded regulated firms that, when dealing with Annex 1 firms, they must carry out due diligence to understand the firm’s business, in accordance with legislative requirements. This includes seeking direct confirmation from the firm of its registration status, conducting independent checks of the information it provides, and understanding and managing any risks.
Registration under the Money Laundering Regulations is not a substitute for regulated firms carrying out their own appropriate due diligence.
Steve Smart, executive director lead for fighting financial crime at the FCA, said: 'We have warned Annex 1 firms that they face increased scrutiny. They must demonstrate they can manage the money laundering risks they face. Where they cannot satisfy us, we will intervene.'
Notes to editors
1. Voluntary restrictions were imposed on Kingscrown Finance Ltd on 21 April 2026, with further voluntary restrictions imposed on 25 September 2026. The further restrictions limit how Kingscrown may receive payments from existing customers and require an orderly wind-down of its existing loan book.
2. On 7 October 2026, voluntary restrictions were imposed on MOMSB Ltd and Momentus Capital Ltd. The restrictions prevent the firms from taking on new customers or entering into new lending arrangements subject to limited exceptions, restrict the circumstances in which they may accept payments from existing customers, and require an independent review of their anti-money laundering framework.
3. On 9 October 2026, voluntary restrictions were imposed on Grosvenor Funding Ltd and Grosvenor Funding (North West) Ltd. The restrictions prevent the firms from taking on new customers or entering into new lending arrangements, restrict the circumstances in which they may accept payments from existing customers, and require an independent review of their anti-money laundering framework.
4. On 15 October 2026, voluntary restrictions were imposed on Abbital Ltd. The restrictions specify the circumstances in which Abbital may take on new customers, enter into new lending arrangements or accept payments from existing customers. They also require an independent review of Abbital’s anti-money laundering systems and controls.
5. Fighting financial crime is one of the FCA's strategic priorities.

publications.title: Agentic AI call for evidence
publications.text:
Agentic AI call for evidence
Start date 8 October 2026
Closing date 20 November 2026
Type ICO consultation
Status Open
The Information Commissioner’s Office is calling for evidence to inform our thinking on how to apply data protection law to the distinctive capabilities and risks of agentic AI.
Your responses will help us identify where we can provide greater clarity or practical support before we publish the final version of the guidance.
We welcome your feedback on the questions in this survey. They are split into the following sections:
Section 1: About you and your organisation
Section 2: Data Security
Section 3: Transparency
Section 4: Accountability
Section 5: Automated Decision Making (ADM)
Section 6: Fairness and purpose limitations
Section 7: Lawfulness of Processing
Section 8: Additional questions
How to respond
You can respond to the call for evidence through Citizen Space.
The consultation will remain open until the end of 20 November 2026. We may not consider responses received after this deadline.

publications.title: Artificial intelligence in UK financial services - 2026
publications.text:
The Bank of England and Financial Conduct Authority conducted a fourth survey of artificial intelligence and machine learning in UK financial services.
7.5: Uncertainty and implementation challenges
The most common governance challenges concerned oversight of third-party AI systems. Applying model risk management principles to third-party or vendor-supplied models was the most frequently selected challenge (54%), followed by overseeing systems provided or materially influenced by third parties (49%).
A second group of challenges concerned the validation and ongoing management of complex or evolving models. Around two-fifths of respondents identified independent validation, ongoing monitoring and drift detection, or change control and versioning as challenges.
Challenges relating to accountability, documentation and senior-manager understanding were reported less frequently. Only a small minority of respondents reported no uncertainty or implementation challenges (Chart 22).
Oversight of third-party AI systems was the most commonly reported area of governance uncertainty or implementation challenge. Applying model risk management principles to third-party or vendor-supplied models was selected by 54% of respondents, while overseeing systems provided or materially influenced by third parties was selected by 49%.
Frontier AI and cyber risk
Most firms expected frontier AI cyber capabilities to become material to their risk profiles. 88% of respondents assessed evolving frontier AI cyber capabilities over the next two years as having a moderate or high impact on their firm’s risk profile.

publications.title: CP26/37: Senior Managers and Certification Regime (SM&CR) Review: Phase 2
publications.text:
CP26/37: Senior Managers and Certification Regime (SM&CR) Review: Phase 2
Consultation open 22/10/2026. Consultation close 22/01/2027.
We’re consulting on changes to streamline and improve the Senior Managers and Certification Regime (SM&CR) as part of the second phase of our reforms.
Why we are consulting
Changes proposed in the Financial Services and Markets (FSM) Bill remove many prescriptive SM&CR requirements from legislation and make regulators responsible for deciding how these should apply in their rules.
Our proposals aim to maintain high standards of individual accountability and conduct while reducing unnecessary burden, making the regime more proportionate and easier to operate.
This consultation builds on the first phase of reforms set out in our Policy Statement (PS26/6).
The main proposals include:
Reducing the number of Senior Management Functions (SMF) applications by removing certain SMFs and making other roles notified.
Streamlining the SMF application process.
Reducing the number of firms subject to the Enhanced regime by raising thresholds.
Removing on-going submissions of Statements of Responsibilities and Management Responsibilities Maps.
Streamlining the Prescribed Responsibilities.
Removing the Certification Regime.
Retiring our Directory of certified and assessed persons.
Simplifying Conduct Rule training and raising breach reporting thresholds.
Who this is for
All firms already in scope of the SM&CR, including third-country branches.
Firms due to come into scope of the SM&CR, such as cryptoasset firms.
Firms regulated by both the PRA and the FCA should also read the PRA’s Consultation Paper CP14/26.
Next steps
Send us your comments by 22 January 2027 using our online response form.
We will review the feedback and expect to publish final regulatory requirements in a Policy Statement in the first half of 2027.
Background
The SM&CR strengthens market integrity and helps reduce consumer harm by making senior managers accountable for their areas of responsibility and setting conduct standards for staff.
The regime has applied to the banking sector since 2016 and was later extended across financial services. We began reviewing it in December 2022. We published first-phase final rules for Phase 1 in Policy Statement PS26/6 in April 2026, alongside the PRA’s PS12/26.

publications.title: Regulatory thresholds set to shift to automatic increases (CP13/26)
publications.text:
Regulatory thresholds set to shift to automatic increases
Proportionality is set to be improved for firms as over 100 regulatory thresholds could be automatically increased periodically.
The Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA) proposes that 128 thresholds across banking, insurance and credit unions increase automatically with nominal Gross Domestic Product (GDP) going forward.
These thresholds cover which regulatory rules apply to firms, how they do so, and what firms are required to report to the PRA.
The proposals would modernise the framework by increasing the proportionality and decreasing the costs of compliance for many firms by replacing the manual ad hoc updates that currently take place. Providing more certainty for firms would assist in their business planning and thereby reduce firms’ barriers to growth.
The largest in-scope threshold is the £320 billion total assets threshold for detailed capital reporting, with the smallest being a £7,500 threshold covering amounts owed to a credit union by an individual. Other significant thresholds involved include the size of an insurer subject to Solvency UK and the Small Domestic Deposit Takers regime total assets threshold.
The first update would take place on 1 July 2031, with further updates occurring every five years thereafter.
The package is expected to benefit all firms, but particularly small and medium sized firms hovering under regulatory thresholds – thereby supporting competition, economic growth and provision of services to the economy.
The consultation opens on 7 October 2026, and closes on 7 February 2027.

publications.title: CP14/26 – Review of the Senior Managers and Certification Regime (SM&CR) – Phase 2
publications.text:
1.1 The Senior Managers and Certification Regime (SM&CR) was introduced in 2016 to strengthen individual accountability for the most senior decision makers in regulated firms. It is one of the principal tools by which the Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA) promotes the safety and soundness of the UK financial system and draws on the lessons learned from the 2008 financial crisis.
1.2 The regime is widely recognised, both domestically and internationally, to have improved individual accountability and prudential standards within firms. By building confidence in the financial system, it has helped to enhance the UK’s position as a leading financial centre.
1.4 The PRA has now identified further opportunities for reform that could achieve similar prudential outcomes at a lower cost to firms. The proposals in this consultation paper (CP) would be the most significant reforms to the regime since its introduction. Building on the Phase 1 reforms, these ‘Phase 2’ proposals anticipate additional regulatory flexibility that would be provided by the Financial Services and Markets Bill 2026 (FSM Bill), if enacted.
8.4 The PRA may share responses to this consultation with the Bank of England, FCA and HM Treasury.
8.5 The PRA invites responses to the proposals set out in this consultation by 22 January 2027.

publications.title: CP26/35: Fair redemption terms for authorised funds investing in illiquid assets
publications.text:
CP26/35: Fair redemption terms for authorised funds investing in illiquid assets
Consultation opens 08/10/2026. Consultation closes 11/12/2026.
We’re consulting on changes to retail investment fund rules so that a fund’s redemption terms reflect the time it typically takes to sell illiquid assets.
Why we are consulting
We want to set clear standards for how firms design and operate their investment products and reduce the risk of people buying unsuitable products. Our proposals will also align these rules with new international standards.
Next steps
We are asking for comments on this Consultation Paper by 11 December 2026.
Following this consultation, we will consider the responses and expect to publish final rules in H1 2027.

publications.title: CP26/34: Preparing for the new transaction reporting regime
publications.text:
CP26/34: Preparing for the new transaction reporting regime
Consultation opens 02/10/2026. Consultation closes 06/11/2026.
We’re consulting on guidance, consequential amendments and transitional provisions to help firms prepare for the new transaction reporting regime.
We have published our draft schema and validation rules to help firms prepare for 3 April 2028.
Who this is for
This consultation will be of interest to:
Investment firms
Operators of trading venues
Approved reporting mechanisms
Trade associations
Other market participants involved in submitting transaction reports, instrument reference data or order book data
Next steps
Please send us your comments by 6 November 2026.

publications.title: GC26/7: Decentralised finance guidance (DeFi)
publications.text:
GC26/7: Decentralised finance guidance (DeFi)
Guidance Consultation opens 21/10/2026. Guidance Consultation closes 18/11/2026.
We’re consulting on non-Handbook guidance to help firms providing financial services using decentralised finance (DeFi) comply with our rules on operational resilience and financial crime, and with the Money Laundering Regulations (MLRs).
Why we are consulting
Our guidance covers observations on the current risk landscape relevant to DeFi. It focuses on operational resilience and financial crime risks, and provides illustrative examples of measures firms may wish to consider.
Firms using DeFi should do so safely and responsibly, as with other technologies. Its features can expose firms and their clients to increased operational resilience and financial crime risks.
From 25 October 2027, the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (Cryptoassets) Regulations 2026 will bring new cryptoasset activities into our regulatory perimeter.

assessments.headline: ICO agentic AI consultation requires Northbridge to review Nudge governance and data protection readiness

impacts.gap: POL-AI governs the Nudge agentic AI pilot but does not yet reflect ICO's emerging expectations on agentic AI autonomy, transparency, and fairness under data protection law.
impacts.action: Review POL-AI against ICO consultation themes (Sections 2–7) and prepare a formal response by the deadline; update model risk tier and validation requirements for M4 if needed.
impacts.dueBasis: ICO call for evidence response deadline
impacts.quote: The Information Commissioner's Office is calling for evidence to inform our thinking on how to apply data protection law to the distinctive capabilities and risks of agentic AI.
impacts.rationale: Northbridge operates an agentic AI collections assistant (Nudge) processing personal data; the ICO consultation will shape future guidance that directly affects model governance and compliance.

impacts.gap: The Nudge pilot DPIA (approved March 2026) may not cover all data protection considerations the ICO is consulting on for agentic AI, such as purpose limitation, automated decision-making transparency, and data security for autonomous agents.
impacts.action: Assess the pilot DPIA against ICO consultation questions; plan a full DPIA update before any Nudge scale-up and feed findings into the quarterly DPIA register review.
impacts.dueBasis: ICO call for evidence response deadline
impacts.quote: The Information Commissioner's Office is calling for evidence to inform our thinking on how to apply data protection law to the distinctive capabilities and risks of agentic AI.
impacts.rationale: The consultation directly targets data protection law application to agentic AI, which is the legal basis for POL-DATA's DPIA requirements and privacy notice obligations for Nudge.

assessments.headline: FCA action on Annex 1 firms demands independent due diligence on non-authorised introducers

impacts.gap: MLR registration status of non-authorised introducers is taken from the introducer's self-declaration and is not independently verified (2025 internal audit open finding).
impacts.action: Replace self-declaration reliance with independent verification of MLR registration status for all non-authorised introducers; update onboarding and annual attestation to require documented evidence from FCA register or OFSI list.
impacts.dueBasis: No explicit deadline in publication; 90-day review period applied from 2026-10-23 press release.
impacts.quote: when dealing with Annex 1 firms, they must carry out due diligence to understand the firm's business, in accordance with legislative requirements. This includes seeking direct confirmation from the firm of its registration status, conducting independent checks of the information it provides, and understanding and managing any risks.
impacts.rationale: The FCA explicitly requires regulated firms to independently verify Annex 1 firms' registration status and information. Northbridge's 60 introducers include non-authorised asset-finance firms that are likely Annex 1 MLR registrants; the current self-declaration control gap is directly exposed by this enforcement action.

impacts.gap: Business-wide risk assessment (C-AML-01) does not explicitly address heightened risk from introducers that are Annex 1 firms; transaction monitoring rules (C-AML-02) do not reference introducer-type risk segmentation.
impacts.action: Refresh the annual business-wide risk assessment to include a specific Annex 1 introducer risk segment; update transaction monitoring rules to flag unusual patterns from introducers subject to FCA MLR supervision.
impacts.dueBasis: No explicit deadline in publication; 90-day review period applied from 2026-10-23 press release.
impacts.quote: The FCA has also reminded regulated firms that, when dealing with Annex 1 firms, they must carry out due diligence to understand the firm's business, in accordance with legislative requirements.
impacts.rationale: The FCA's information request to ~900 Annex 1 firms and warning of increased scrutiny means Northbridge must demonstrate it understands and manages ML risks from its Annex 1 introducer population in its own risk assessment and monitoring.

impacts.gap: Annual review of critical suppliers (C-TPR-01) and financial crime controls testing (C-TPR-03) do not currently treat non-authorised introducers as critical third parties requiring independent MLR status verification.
impacts.action: Classify non-authorised introducers as critical third parties for AML purposes; enhance annual review and financial crime controls testing to include independent verification of their MLR registration and AML control effectiveness.
impacts.dueBasis: No explicit deadline in publication; 90-day review period applied from 2026-10-23 press release.
impacts.quote: Registration under the Money Laundering Regulations is not a substitute for regulated firms carrying out their own appropriate due diligence.
impacts.rationale: Introducers are key partners in the lending chain; the FCA's statement that MLR registration does not substitute for regulated firms' own due diligence extends third-party risk management obligations to cover introducer AML controls.

assessments.headline: FCA Financial Crime Guide consultation impacts AML, fraud, third-party controls

impacts.gap: Policy follows the Financial Crime Guide as external standard; proposed updates to sanctions, proliferation financing (currently not separately assessed), ML/TF and systems/controls require refreshed business risk assessment and transaction monitoring rules.
impacts.action: Review consultation proposals against current business risk assessment and transaction monitoring rules; prepare response by 24 December 2026 and plan policy updates for final Guide.
impacts.quote: We're proposing changes to the following areas: fraud cryptoassets – to reflect new regime from October 2027 financial and trade sanctions proliferation financing data security financial crime systems and controls money laundering and terrorist financing
impacts.rationale: The Financial Crime Guide is explicitly referenced in POL-AML; multiple proposed updates directly affect its core domains including sanctions screening, proliferation financing gap, and ML/TF systems.

impacts.gap: Policy references the Financial Crime Guide fraud chapter as its external standard; proposed fraud chapter updates will require refresh of the fraud typologies library and potentially other fraud controls.
impacts.action: Map consultation fraud proposals against current fraud typologies library and controls; submit feedback and schedule library update once final Guide published.
impacts.quote: We want firms to keep detecting, preventing and disrupting financial crime, so we can protect consumers and maintain trust in the financial system
impacts.rationale: Fraud is the first-listed area of proposed Guide changes; POL-FRAUD explicitly adopts the Guide fraud chapter as its benchmark.

impacts.gap: Critical third parties (KYC vendor, sanctions screening vendor) supply financial crime controls; consultation highlights AI and third-party tools for financial crime controls as an emerging risk area not yet fully addressed in annual review or independent testing requirements.
impacts.action: Enhance annual critical supplier review and independent testing programme to cover Guide expectations for AI/third-party financial crime tools; include in consultation response.
impacts.quote: firms have increasingly adopted AI and third-party tools for financial crime controls
impacts.rationale: Northbridge relies on third-party KYC and sanctions screening vendors for core financial crime controls; the Guide update signals supervisory focus on oversight of such tools.

assessments.headline: BoE/FCA AI survey exposes vendor model oversight gaps

impacts.gap: Policy states 'Vendor models: Northbridge relies on vendor validation reports; independent validation of vendor models is not currently performed' and drift monitoring (C-AI-02) covers only M1/M2 monthly and M4 weekly QA, not independent validation or comprehensive third-party model oversight.
impacts.action: Add independent validation requirement for vendor-supplied models (M1 credit scorecard, M4 LLM API) and extend drift monitoring to cover third-party model change control and versioning.
impacts.dueBasis: 90 days from publication date 2026-10-26 as no regulatory deadline specified
impacts.quote: Applying model risk management principles to third-party or vendor-supplied models was the most frequently selected challenge (54%), followed by overseeing systems provided or materially influenced by third parties (49%).
impacts.rationale: The survey identifies vendor model oversight as the top governance challenge (54%), directly exposing Northbridge's reliance on vendor assurance without independent validation for M1 and M4.

impacts.gap: C-TPR-03 only requires annual testing of financial crime controls from third parties; it does not extend to AI model governance for the LLM API provider (critical third party) or credit bureau scorecard vendor.
impacts.action: Expand annual critical supplier reviews (C-TPR-01) to include AI model risk management assessment for LLM API provider and credit bureau vendor, aligning with POL-AI requirements.
impacts.dueBasis: 90 days from publication date 2026-10-26 as no regulatory deadline specified
impacts.quote: Overseeing systems provided or materially influenced by third parties was selected by 49%.
impacts.rationale: Nearly half of firms report challenges overseeing third-party-influenced systems; Northbridge's LLM API provider and credit bureau are critical third parties whose AI systems need oversight beyond financial crime controls.

impacts.gap: Annual penetration test (C-SEC-01) and quarterly access reviews (C-SEC-02) do not explicitly address frontier AI-driven cyber threats or AI-enhanced attack vectors.
impacts.action: Update penetration testing scope and access review criteria to include AI-specific threat scenarios (e.g., prompt injection, model extraction, AI-generated phishing) for systems using third-party AI (Nudge, KYC vendor).
impacts.dueBasis: 90 days from publication date 2026-10-26 as no regulatory deadline specified
impacts.quote: Most firms expected frontier AI cyber capabilities to become material to their risk profiles. 88% of respondents assessed evolving frontier AI cyber capabilities over the next two years as having a moderate or high impact on their firm's risk profile.
impacts.rationale: The survey signals a near-consensus that AI-enhanced cyber risk will be material within two years; Northbridge's AI-assisted collections (Nudge) and vendor AI systems expand the attack surface.

assessments.headline: FCA SM&CR Phase 2 consultation proposes regime simplification affecting Northbridge governance

impacts.gap: Policy requires annual certification cycle (C-GOV-01), six-monthly Statements of Responsibilities reviews (C-GOV-02), and Conduct Rules training completion above 98% (C-GOV-03); consultation proposes removing Certification Regime, ending ongoing Statements of Responsibilities and Management Responsibilities Map submissions, and simplifying Conduct Rule training.
impacts.action: Review consultation proposals against POL-GOV controls, prepare formal response by 22 January 2027, and draft policy updates for implementation upon final rules in H1 2027.
impacts.quote: Changes proposed in the Financial Services and Markets (FSM) Bill remove many prescriptive SM&CR requirements from legislation and make regulators responsible for deciding how these should apply in their rules.
impacts.rationale: The consultation proposes fundamental changes to SM&CR including removal of Certification Regime, ongoing Statements of Responsibilities submissions, and simplified Conduct Rules, all directly affecting POL-GOV controls C-GOV-01, C-GOV-02, C-GOV-03 and the Management Responsibilities Map process.

impacts.gap: Policy governs Nudge (M4) but lacks reference to ICO agentic AI or foundation model guidance expectations for governance, transparency, and vendor oversight.
impacts.action: Monitor ICO agentic AI and foundation model consultations; schedule POL-AI review upon final guidance publication in Autumn 2026.
